title: 1.2.31 Module 1.2 Quiz
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on dynamic typing, the seven primitives, and null vs undefined. Checked instantly.

questions.question: What does it mean that JavaScript is "dynamically typed"?
options: Every variable must be given a type when you declare it
A variable can only ever hold one kind of value
You never say what type a variable is, and the same variable can hold a different kind of value later
JavaScript works out the answer before the program runs
questions.explanation: You never write the type. `let x = 10;` then `x = "ten";` is perfectly legal — the value carries the type, not the variable.

questions.question: Which list names the seven primitive data types in JavaScript?
options: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, bigint, symbol
string, number, boolean, array, object, function, null
int, float, char, string, boolean, array, object
text, number, yes/no, empty, missing, big number, name
questions.explanation: Those seven. Arrays, objects and functions are not primitives — they are objects, which is the other half of the primitive/object split.

questions.question: What are the three special numeric values?
options: Zero, one and minus one
null, undefined and NaN
Infinity, -Infinity and NaN
Infinity, BigInt and NaN
questions.explanation: Infinity and -Infinity come from going past what a number can hold (or dividing by zero); NaN comes from arithmetic that has no numeric answer. `null` and `undefined` are not numbers at all.

questions.question: What does `typeof NaN` give you?
options: "NaN"
"number"
"undefined"
"error"
questions.explanation: NaN stands for "not a number", but it is still of type number — it is the number type's way of saying "this calculation had no numeric answer".

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
options: They are the same thing written two ways
undefined is what JavaScript leaves when nothing has been put there; null is emptiness you set on purpose
null is what JavaScript leaves; undefined is what you set on purpose
undefined is for numbers and null is for strings
questions.explanation: Who put it there is the difference. Seeing undefined usually means a value never arrived; seeing null means somebody deliberately said "nothing here right now".

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: An error — you cannot put a string in a number variable
ten
undefined
questions.explanation: It prints ten. JavaScript is dynamically typed, so reassigning x to a string is allowed — the variable never had a type to violate.

questions.question: What can a backtick string do that a double-quote string cannot?
options: Hold more characters
Be compared with ===
Drop a value straight into the text with ${...}
Contain the letter n
questions.explanation: Backticks give you template literals: `${name}` puts the value of name right into the text. In double quotes, ${name} is just those characters.

questions.question: What does `typeof null` give you, and what is odd about it?
options: "null" — nothing odd, that is the type name
"undefined" — odd, because null and undefined are different
"object" — odd, because null is not an object; it is a long-standing mistake in the language
"empty" — odd, because that type does not otherwise exist
questions.explanation: It answers "object", which is wrong — null is a primitive. It is a bug from the very first version of JavaScript that was never fixed, because fixing it would break existing sites.
